title: The shape of a split

blocks.text: The page asks you to **draw the recursion tree** for an array size and a threshold, and contrasts a **balanced** (50/50) split with an **unbalanced** (10/90) one, whose tree is deeper and has more tasks. Page 6.6.1.2 estimates a midpoint split's tree as depth `d = ceil(log2(N / T))`, `2^d` leaves and `2^(d+1) - 1` tasks; that estimate is exact only when every halving is even.
Write `SplitTree.shape(n, threshold, percent)`. It walks the split of the range `[0, n)` exactly as a task would and returns its `Shape(depth, leaves, tasks)`:

items: a range of at most `threshold` elements is a **leaf**;
a longer range `[start, end)` splits at `start + (end - start) * percent / 100`; if that is not past `start`, it splits at `start + 1`, so the recursion always makes progress;
`depth` is the deepest leaf's level (the root is level 0), `leaves` counts leaves, `tasks` counts every range, leaves included.

cases.says: A midpoint split of 10,000 elements with threshold 1,000 has depth 4, 16 leaves and 31 tasks.
A range of exactly threshold elements is one leaf and one task, at depth 0.
A 10/90 split makes a much deeper tree with more tasks than a midpoint split of the same range.
When percent of a short range rounds down to 0, the split still moves at least one element to the left.
An odd split is counted as it really happens, where the 2^d estimate would be wrong.

concepts: A 50/50 split makes a shallow tree of about log2(N/T) levels, while a 10/90 split makes a deeper tree with more tasks.
The recursion tree for an array size and threshold can be drawn: a range of at most the threshold is a leaf, and each split adds a level.
